visuals.title: What overdose can hit
visuals.text: CNS depression, respiratory failure, arrhythmia, seizures and organ failure (for example the liver in paracetamol).

visuals.title: Signature features by drug
head: Drug
Key clue
rows: Pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, low GCS

visual.caption: QRS over 100 ms raises seizure risk; over 160 ms, ventricular arrhythmias.
visual.label: Example: 130 ms

visual.caption: Respiratory centre stimulation causes alkalosis first; uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation then adds metabolic acidosis.

glossary.Self-harm: Intentionally injuring or poisoning oneself, with or without the intent to die.
glossary.Recreational: Drug use for pleasure rather than medical need.
glossary.CNS depression: Slowing of brain function, causing drowsiness, reduced consciousness and slowed breathing.
glossary.Respiratory failure: The lungs cannot keep oxygen up or carbon dioxide down to safe levels.
glossary.Seizures: Episodes of abnormal brain electrical activity causing fits or altered awareness.
glossary.Organ failure: An organ such as the liver or kidney no longer able to do its job.
glossary.ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity.
glossary.Paracetamol: A common painkiller that is toxic to the liver in overdose.
glossary.RUQ: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen, over the liver.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellowing of the skin and eyes from raised bilirubin, often a sign of liver damage.
glossary.Anorexia nervosa: An eating disorder with dangerously low weight; low glutathione stores increase paracetamol toxicity.
glossary.HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which weakens the immune system.
glossary.Malnutrition: Poor nutrition, lowering the liver's glutathione stores.
glossary.Rifampicin: An antibiotic for TB that induces liver P450 enzymes.
glossary.Phenytoin: An anti-epileptic drug that induces liver P450 enzymes.
glossary.Carbamazepine: An anti-epileptic drug that induces liver P450 enzymes.
glossary.Opioid: Morphine-like drugs, such as heroin, codeine and oxycodone, acting on opioid receptors.
glossary.Respiratory depression: Slow, shallow breathing that fails to clear carbon dioxide.
glossary.Benzodiazepine: Sedative drugs such as diazepam that enhance GABA, the brain's calming signal.
glossary.Ataxia: Unsteadiness and poor coordination of movement.
glossary.Aspirin: Acetylsalicylic acid, a painkiller and antiplatelet drug.
glossary.Bradycardia: Heart rate below 60 beats per minute.
glossary.Coma: Deep unconsciousness from which the patient cannot be roused.
glossary.Tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
glossary.Acidosis: Too much acid in the blood, pH below 7.35.
glossary.PR: The ECG interval from the start of atrial to the start of ventricular activation.
glossary.QT: The ECG interval covering ventricular depolarisation and repolarisation; prolonged QT risks arrhythmia.
glossary.Antihistamines: Allergy drugs that block histamine; older ones have strong anticholinergic effects.
glossary.Cocaine: An illegal stimulant that blocks reuptake of noradrenaline and dopamine.
glossary.Amphetamines: Stimulant drugs that release noradrenaline and dopamine.
glossary.Salivation: Producing saliva; excessive in cholinergic poisoning.
glossary.Blood gases: Tests of blood pH, oxygen, carbon dioxide and bicarbonate.
glossary.Cardiotoxic: Damaging to the heart or its rhythm.
glossary.12-lead ECG: The standard full ECG, recording the heart from 12 views.
glossary.Conservative management: Watching and supporting the patient without specific active treatment.
glossary.Recovery position: Lying an unconscious, breathing patient on their side to keep the airway clear.
glossary.CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths in cardiac arrest.
glossary.Atropine: A drug that blocks the vagus nerve, raising a slow heart rate.
glossary.Glucagon: A hormone that raises heart rate and contractility independently of beta receptors.
glossary.Beta-blocker: Drugs such as bisoprolol that slow the heart and lower blood pressure.
glossary.Vitamin K: A vitamin needed to make clotting factors; reverses warfarin.
glossary.Warfarin: An oral anticoagulant that blocks vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
glossary.Plasma concentration: The level of a drug in the blood.
glossary.ALT: Alanine aminotransferase, a liver enzyme that rises with liver cell damage.
glossary.Non-IgE: Not caused by IgE antibodies, so not true allergy, though it can look similar.
glossary.Salbutamol: A bronchodilator that opens the airways.
glossary.Nebulised: Given as a mist breathed in through a mask.
glossary.Sodium bicarbonate: An alkali given IV to raise blood pH and urine pH.
glossary.Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung air spaces causing breathlessness.
glossary.Dialysis: Artificially removing toxins, acid and fluid from the blood.
glossary.Toxicology: The specialty dealing with poisons and overdoses.
glossary.Conjugation: Joining a molecule to another, such as glutathione, to make it harmless and excretable.
glossary.Respiratory centre: The area in the brainstem that controls the rate and depth of breathing.
glossary.Hyperventilation: Breathing faster or deeper than needed, blowing off carbon dioxide.
glossary.Oxidative phosphorylation: The process in mitochondria that makes ATP using oxygen.
glossary.Lactic: Relating to lactic acid, produced when cells cannot use oxygen to make energy.
glossary.Myocytes: Muscle cells; cardiac myocytes are heart muscle cells.
glossary.Phase 0 depolarisation: The rapid upstroke of the cardiac action potential, driven by sodium entering the cell.
glossary.Agonism: A drug binding to and activating a receptor.
glossary.Brainstem: The base of the brain controlling breathing, heart rate and consciousness.
glossary.Antagonist: A drug that binds a receptor and blocks it without activating it.
glossary.Neurotransmitter: A chemical messenger passing signals between nerve cells.
glossary.Acetylcholinesterase: The enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine; blocking it causes cholinergic excess.
